lastText: File ClosedTanks Kept for Egypt, and Not EnoughContestedAllied Combined Chiefs, 1940–1945End of hostilities: NOVEMBER 1945 (PROJECTED) · filed out of sequence, pages missingImmediate AftermathVictory in Europe arrives around November 1945: slower than the historical May 1945, the price of caution at the moments this campaign offered a faster, riskier road instead. The campaign reaches its end having spent more Western Allied lives than the historical record: the price of the bolder, more aggressive road at several of this campaign's genuine forks. The February 1945 eastern-city raids were declined: Dresden never becomes the word it became, and the oil and rail campaigns finished the war's arithmetic without it, exactly as their own advocates' logic implied they could. The Morgenthau Plan's deindustrialization policy was actually pursued rather than quietly abandoned: testing the humanitarian and economic consequences Stimson warned about directly. The Ljubljana Gap drive toward Vienna was actually attempted: Churchill's political-geography thesis run against the mountains and the single-track railway every American planner cited against it. What was really being decided, choice by choice, was never whether Germany lost, only what the peace on the other side of it would look like.One Year LaterA year past victory in Europe, the machinery of occupation is running on the arrangements this campaign's own conferences (Tehran, Yalta, the ones this command actually attended) settled
